title: Asylum activity relative to population
text:
A country’s size changes how an application total should be read. This page divides reported asylum activity by the receiving country’s population in the same year, showing both events per 100,000 residents and the inverse, residents per recorded event.
Population comes from the World Bank’s SP.POP.TOTL indicator: annual midyear estimates. World Bank definition and sources. A missing population or asylum value remains unavailable; another year’s population is never substituted.
populationData=FileAttachment("data/population/comparison.json").json()
popCore=import((await FileAttachment("assets/population-core.js").url())+"?v=1")
viewof populationCountry=Inputs.select(populationData.countries,{label:"Receiving country",format:d=>popCore.countryName(d)+" ("+d.iso+")",value:populationData.countries.find(d=>d.iso===(new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get("country")||"GBR"))||populationData.countries[0]})

viewof populationMode=Inputs.radio(new Map([["Person-reported records (comparable population basis)","P"],["All reported activity (persons + cases; exploratory)","combined"]]),{label:"Numerator coverage",value:"P"})
viewof populationMetric=Inputs.select(popCore.metrics,{label:"Trend and country-comparison measure",format:d=>d[1],value:popCore.metrics[0]})
populationRows=popCore.countryYears(populationData,populationCountry.iso,populationMode)
populationSelected=populationRows.find(d=>d.year===populationYear)
populationMetricKey=populationMetric[0]+"_per_100k"
populationTable=popCore.metrics.map(([key,label])=>({measure:label,count:populationSelected[key],population:populationSelected.population,population_year:populationSelected.population_year,per_100k:populationSelected[key+"_per_100k"],residents_per_event:populationSelected["residents_per_"+key]}))
populationComparison=populationData.top20.map(iso=>({...popCore.countryYears(populationData,iso,populationMode).find(d=>d.year===populationYear),name:popCore.countryName(populationData.countries.find(c=>c.iso===iso)||{iso,name:iso})})).sort((a,b)=>(b[populationMetricKey]??-1)-(a[populationMetricKey]??-1))
{
  const note=document.createElement("p");note.className="explorer-status";
  note.textContent=populationCountry.name+" · "+populationYear+" population: "+(populationSelected.population?populationSelected.population.toLocaleString("en-GB"):"unavailable for this year")+". Coverage: "+(populationMode==="P"?"person-reported activity only":"mixed persons/cases activity; exploratory")+". Population reference year: "+(populationSelected.population_year??"unavailable")+".";
  return note;
}

title: Processing Productivity
text: How does recorded decision output compare with incoming application volume? These charts use the notebook’s decision-to-application ratio, expressed as decisions per 100 applications.

title: Processing Productivity
text:
How to read the charts
100 means as many decisions as applications were recorded in that year. Above 100 means decisions exceeded applications; below 100 means applications exceeded decisions. These comparisons alone do not establish whether a backlog grew or fell.
The pale line shows each annual ratio; the teal line is a three-year centred mean of annual ratios, using available values at the ends. A missing annual ratio remains a gap. This is an average of ratios, not a ratio of three-year totals. No ratio is calculated when applications are zero or either flow is unavailable.
Reporting units: original persons- and case-reported values are added without conversion in both flows. These exploratory ratios can be affected by different unit mixes and reporting coverage; they are not harmonised comparisons of people or a league table of national efficiency.
Selection: the same Top 20 receiving countries as the Country Explorer gallery, ranked by combined reported application volume across 2000–2025. This is the fixed notebook edition, rather than the explorer’s refreshed dataset.

title: Processing Productivity
section: Who is keeping pace, and who is falling behind?
text:
Who is keeping pace, and who is falling behind?
A stronger recorded flow balance is not the same as having everything under control. These data show output relative to inflow, but not whether a country has cleared its pending caseload, shortened waits, or improved decision quality. All recorded decisions, including closures, count as output.

Stronger flow balances
Germany (102), Sweden (117), Switzerland (102). The figures in brackets are decisions per 100 applications across 2021–2025, calculated from summed counts. Each of these countries also reached at least 100 across 2023–2025 and in 2025, with shortfalls in no more than two of the five years. That is evidence of a stronger recent balance in reported activity, rather than proof of an efficient or backlog-free system.
France illustrates the difference between a period balance and the latest year: it recorded 109 decisions per 100 applications over 2021–2025, but 98 in 2025. Its multi-year output exceeded inflow, while the latest year was slightly below balance.


Repeated shortfalls
United States (40), Italy (61), Canada (59), Egypt (15), Belgium (78), Mexico (65), Kenya (31), Netherlands (71). Each had applications exceeding decisions in at least four of the five years, and fewer than 100 decisions per 100 applications in both the five-year and recent three-year totals. Repeated imbalances suggest sustained processing pressure; the size of an actual pending caseload must be established from stock data.


Which balances have deteriorated?
Comparing 2018–2020 with 2023–2025, the following complete-coverage countries were below balance in the recent period and fell by at least 10 decisions per 100 applications: Italy, 209 → 58; Egypt, 100 → 11; Kenya, 112 → 30; Canada, 80 → 52; United States, 56 → 42; Belgium, 95 → 82. This is a deterioration in the output-to-inflow ratio, not evidence that staff became less productive: faster application growth can lower the ratio even when decision volumes increase.
The Netherlands and Mexico also have repeated shortfalls, but their recent ratios improved relative to 2018–2020. Still behind and getting further behind are different findings.
The Russian Federation was close to balance, rather than clearly in catch-up: 99.9 decisions per 100 applications in 2021?2025 and 100.4 in 2023?2025. The small difference should not be given more weight than reporting precision allows.


Catch-up and misleading averages
United Kingdom (92), Austria (97) show recent catch-up: five-year output was below inflow, but 2023–2025 output exceeded inflow. For the UK this was 92 decisions per 100 applications across 2021–2025, versus 116 across 2023–2025. Recent output can be clearing older claims, so a favourable ratio does not establish that pending claims have disappeared.
Peru needs particular care. Its high five-year ratio is dominated by 136,383 recorded decisions in 2023, followed by 1,318 in 2024 and 1,897 in 2025. Across 2021–2025, approximately 95% of its recorded decisions were closures. This is not evidence of consistently high substantive decision output; the table labels it a mixed annual pattern.
Coverage prevents a confident classification for South Africa and Türkiye. South Africa lacks application volume in 2021; Türkiye lacks decision volume in 2024 and 2025. Their available-year ratios are shown in the table, with the denominator’s coverage, but excluded from the complete five-year chart. High output in the years available does not fill those gaps.



Recorded decisions per 100 applications across 2021–2025 for the 18 Top 20 receiving countries with paired flows in all five years.




The full comparison
All three numeric period columns show decisions per 100 applications. Values close to the threshold of 100 retain one decimal so rounding does not hide which side of balance they fall on. Period ratios divide summed decisions by summed applications for years with both flows available; they do not average annual ratios. A shortfall year has fewer recorded decisions than applications. Classification is descriptive, based on the explicit thresholds above, and is not a statistical test or an efficiency ranking.

text:
Annual shortfalls and country waterfalls
Coral: applications exceed decisions. Teal: decisions exceed applications. The first panel shows each annual difference; the waterfall adds these differences from a zero opening balance in 2000. Missing annual reports remain gaps and stop cumulative calculations.

About the old “minimum backlog” figures
The final panel is explicitly illustrative, not an observed backlog or a defensible lower bound on it. It follows balance[t] = max(0, balance[t−1] + applications[t] − decisions[t]), starting at zero. It assumes compatible flow units, scope, and timing and no other entries, exits, transfers, or reporting adjustments. The combined persons/cases records do not establish those assumptions. Compare actual unresolved caseloads using the separately observed UNHCR stocks on the front page.


What if the gap persists?
If reported applications continue to exceed comparable recorded decisions, processing pressure will persist unless inflows fall or output rises. This is a conditional scenario, not a prediction that every country will worsen. The record includes years and countries where decisions exceeded applications. Resource needs, future inflows, and policy changes are not modelled here.

title: Worldwide asylum trends
section: The worldwide pattern: growth, peaks and processing pressure
text:
The worldwide pattern: growth, peaks and processing pressure
Reported applications rose from 2,245,518 in 2019 to 3,343,203 in 2025. Applications in 2025 were 49% higher than in 2019 (2,245,518). The recent expansion was not a continuous rise: the series peaked at 3,848,894 in 2023. Applications in 2025 were 2.3% lower than in 2024 (3,421,776). This distinction matters: a high level of demand and a growing unresolved caseload can coexist with a fall in new applications.
In 2025, 2,836,187 decisions were recorded against 3,343,203 applications: 85 decisions per 100 applications. Applications exceeded decisions in 16 of the 26 years. Persistent shortfalls indicate processing pressure, although the difference is not an observed backlog. The separate end-year stock series is the appropriate evidence for unresolved claims; see what remains unresolved.
The stock of unresolved claims has also expanded. The separately reported end-year asylum-seeker population rose from 4,148,141 in 2019 to 8,998,097 in 2025 (117% higher), including a 7.7% rise from 2024. Unlike the mixed-unit application totals, this stock is reported in persons. It is not obtained by summing annual flow gaps.
Read the changes as reported activity. The series combines persons and cases, application types and procedures, and changing source coverage. It counts application events rather than unique people. Growth in these totals cannot on its own identify the causes of migration, demonstrate onward movement, or establish that future pressure must increase.

3. What remains unresolved?
Subtracting annual decisions from applications can be tempting. But the result is a difference between flows—not a count of unresolved claims.
Here we use UNHCR’s observed end-year asylum-seeker stock, reported in persons. This retains its original population unit; it is not an application count. This is a separate population series, reported at a date. It is not reconstructed by adding up the gaps between the bars in the first figure.






Figure 2: Observed UNHCR worldwide end-year asylum-seeker stocks, reported in persons from 2000 to 2025.




What to take from this: use observed stocks when asking how many claims are pending. Annual applications minus decisions cannot establish a reconciled backlog, and these data do not provide individual waiting times.

Before interpreting the latest year, check who reported
A worldwide sum can change because of the records available, as well as because of underlying events. One practical check is to count receiving-country codes represented in each year’s data.
In 2025, the saved application data includes 139 receiving-country codes, compared with 154 in 2024. Decision data includes 142, compared with 152. Each code is counted once per year in each file, regardless of application volume or whether the record uses persons or cases. A record with zero reported volume still counts as reporting presence. These panels show how widely the data covers receiving countries, not how many applications were received.

This does not tell us which explanation accounts for a change in volume. It does tell us why a lower recorded total should not automatically become a claim that worldwide demand has fallen by the same proportion.

title: Worldwide asylum trends
text:
Understanding processing pressure
The processing story has three parts: incoming applications, recorded decision output, and the separately observed unresolved caseload:

Applications: how many application events were recorded, and of which types?
Decisions: what outcomes did reporting authorities record?
Pending claims: what unresolved stock was observed at the reporting date?

They do not, by themselves, explain national policy differences, measure an applicant’s chance of recognition, or establish how long people wait.

Go further: Read the methods and sources, inspect the full analysis notebook, or explore UNHCR’s methodology.

Report summary · Saved data through 2025
The recorded 2025 flow gap was 507,016: that many more applications than decisions were reported. This is an imbalance between annual flows, not an estimate of the backlog. The pending headline above comes from a separate observed population series.

title: Asylum under pressure
text:
The main findings

High demand, despite a retreat from the peak. Applications in 2025 were 49% above 2019, but 2.3% below 2024. The recorded peak was 3.8m in 2023. Recent growth has not been uninterrupted. Explore the worldwide trends.
The unresolved stock has grown faster. The observed asylum-seeker stock rose 117% since 2019, and 7.7% from 2024 to 2025. It is a persons-based population measure, distinct from mixed-unit application events. See the stock series.
Processing pressure is uneven. Some receiving countries have recorded enough output to match recent inflow; others have repeated shortfalls. Period totals, annual variation and closures all matter. Read the processing assessment.
Protection rates differ sharply. The same recorded nationality can have very different aggregate outcomes in different receiving countries, and rates can change substantially over time. Different claim circumstances, procedures and timing prevent interpreting these as individual chances or isolated policy effects. Compare grant rates and recent changes.

How protection rates differ and change
An overall rate mixes policy, procedure and the claims being decided. A change can arise because the nationalities or types of claims changed, because older claims were decided, or because decision practices changed. The descriptive comparisons below establish differences, not their causes. Closures are excluded from substantive rates and shown separately on this page.

Largest recent changes in the Top 20
These are the five largest absolute 2024–2025 changes among the fixed Top 20 receiving countries with complete, reconciled annual totals and at least 500 substantive decisions in both years. Selection by change is descriptive; it is not a statistical significance test. Missing or unreconciled years are excluded.

United States: protection rate 58% in 2024 → 23% in 2025 (-34.2 percentage points); substantive decisions 61,911 → 148,216.
Netherlands: protection rate 76% in 2024 → 48% in 2025 (-27.7 percentage points); substantive decisions 21,154 → 15,397.
Germany: protection rate 53% in 2024 → 34% in 2025 (-19.5 percentage points); substantive decisions 263,789 → 279,201.
Belgium: protection rate 45% in 2024 → 27% in 2025 (-17.8 percentage points); substantive decisions 37,782 → 34,718.
Austria: protection rate 80% in 2024 → 63% in 2025 (-16.7 percentage points); substantive decisions 30,963 → 18,622.

Grey means unavailable, not zero. These are outcome shares, not cohort success rates or the substantive recognition rates above. Changes across origin, destination, and year do not by themselves establish discrimination or policy effects: procedure, case mix, reporting units, and coverage also vary.
The 2025 panels place application volumes beside decision outcomes on separate axes, avoiding the original overlapping scales. Decisions need not concern the applications recorded in that year. title: UK asylum: comparing the sources
text:
What the UK trends show
The Home Office calendar-year series records 101,911 people claiming asylum in 2025, compared with 45,537 in 2019 (124% higher). In 2025 it recorded 135,740 initial decisions. Initial decision output exceeded that year’s claims, but those decisions include claims lodged earlier; this is not the fraction of 2025 applicants who were processed.
The published main-applicant initial grant rate was 42% in 2025, versus 52% in 2019. This official rate has its own applicant scope: it should not be reconstructed from the all-people grant and decision counts. The separately dated small-boat rates below concern a specific arrival group, rather than everyone claiming asylum in the UK.
Cross-country context uses the broader UNHCR extract. On that common reported-activity basis, the UK recorded 168,185 applications and 194,877 decisions in 2025, or 116 decisions per 100 applications. The corresponding ratios were Germany (124), France (98), Canada (72). These contrasts show flows relative to demand, not staff efficiency or waiting times. They combine persons and cases and different procedure mixes; the first-instance persons-only comparison below has a deliberately narrower scope.

Match the period and the measure first
This comparison deliberately uses UNHCR first-instance (FI), persons-reported (P) rows for the UK, rather than the combined-unit, all-procedure totals elsewhere in the report. Appeals and other stages are excluded. The Home Office separates initial decisions from withdrawals and other administrative outcomes; the UNHCR comparison decision count therefore sums refugee recognition, complementary protection, and rejection, excluding closures.
